reference.source: Sherlock's Diseases of the Liver and Biliary System / EBMT-EASL guidance
clinicalPearls: Classically follows myeloablative haematopoietic stem-cell transplantation, but is also caused by pyrrolizidine-alkaloid herbal teas and certain chemotherapeutic and immunotoxin agents
The hallmark triad is tender hepatomegaly, unexplained weight gain with fluid retention/ascites, and hyperbilirubinaemia arising in the early weeks after conditioning
Diagnosis is largely clinical using established criteria (modified Seattle/Baltimore or paediatric EBMT), supported by imaging rather than a single confirmatory test
Doppler ultrasound may show hepatomegaly, ascites, gallbladder-wall oedema and reversed or absent portal venous flow, though early findings can be non-specific
A raised hepatic venous pressure gradient and characteristic transjugular biopsy help in uncertain or severe cases when the risk is justified
Defibrotide is used for severe SOS, alongside meticulous fluid and sodium management and avoidance of further hepatotoxins
Severity is graded (mild to very severe) by the degree of bilirubin rise, weight gain, and multi-organ dysfunction, which guides urgency of treatment
reference.pathophysiology: The primary injury is to hepatic sinusoidal endothelial cells and downstream zone-3 hepatocytes, damaged by conditioning chemoradiotherapy, pyrrolizidine alkaloids, or other toxins. Endothelial denudation and sloughing obstruct sinusoidal blood flow, and subendothelial oedema with fibrin deposition narrows the terminal hepatic venules. The resulting post-sinusoidal outflow obstruction produces portal hypertension, hepatocellular necrosis and cholestasis, clinically manifest as tender hepatomegaly, weight gain, ascites and jaundice, and in severe disease progressing to hepatorenal and multi-organ failure.
additionalDifferentials: Fungal or viral hepatitis in the immunosuppressed host
Capillary leak or engraftment syndrome causing fluid overload
additionalInvestigations: Serial bilirubin, transaminases and weight/fluid-balance monitoring against diagnostic criteria
Doppler ultrasound of the liver assessing hepatomegaly, ascites and portal/hepatic venous flow
Full blood count and coagulation studies including markers of endothelial activation
Hepatic venous pressure gradient measurement in selected uncertain cases
Transjugular liver biopsy when the diagnosis remains in doubt and bleeding risk allows
Screening for concurrent infection and graft-versus-host disease
redFlags: Rapidly rising bilirubin with renal or respiratory dysfunction indicating very severe multi-organ SOS
Refractory fluid retention and tense ascites with encephalopathy
Progressive hepatomegaly and pain suggesting fulminant hepatic failure
New coagulopathy or falling platelet transfusion increments signalling worsening endothelial injury
reference.prognosis: Mild and moderate SOS often resolves with supportive care, but severe or very severe disease with multi-organ failure carries a high mortality; early recognition and timely use of defibrotide improve outcomes.
pitfalls: Attributing early weight gain and jaundice to sepsis or graft-versus-host disease and delaying diagnosis
Relying on a single imaging feature, since early Doppler findings are frequently normal or non-specific
Overloading the patient with fluids and sodium, worsening ascites and outflow congestion
Continuing nephrotoxic or hepatotoxic drugs that compound endothelial injury
Forgetting non-transplant causes such as pyrrolizidine-alkaloid ingestion in patients using herbal remedies
references: Sherlock's Diseases of the Liver and Biliary System
EBMT/EASL guidance on hepatic sinusoidal obstruction syndrome
management: Defibrotide for severe or very severe disease, the principal disease-directed therapy
Meticulous fluid and sodium restriction with diuretics to control fluid overload and ascites while preserving renal perfusion
Avoidance of further hepatotoxins and careful review of concurrent nephrotoxic and hepatotoxic drugs
Risk-factor mitigation and prophylaxis with ursodeoxycholic acid in high-risk myeloablative transplant recipients
Supportive and organ support including analgesia, paracentesis for tense ascites, and renal replacement or respiratory support in multi-organ failure
Serial bilirubin, weight and fluid-balance monitoring with Doppler ultrasound against diagnostic criteria, and screening for concurrent infection and graft-versus-host disease
Escalation to intensive care and transplant hepatology for severe or multi-organ disease
